rationale: This sample is the Shootout strcat benchmark: a very small C++ program dominated by a tight, hot string-concatenation loop, with no source-level feature data available, so the table leans on the benchmark's known characteristics. Runtime in such benchmarks is dominated by inner-loop iterations, so passes with near-zero execution overhead are weighted highest: SUB (cheap instruction substitution, strong security-per-byte), SPLIT (pure layout change), and IGV/ICALL (cheap global-value and call indirection that also add good binary-level diversity with essentially no loop-body cost). IBR is kept at a moderate weight since its dispatch overhead lands inside hot loops but it materially disrupts static control-flow recovery. BCF and FLA are retained but with lowered SecurityGain/DiversityGain weights and elevated RuntimeCost/SizeCost weights, so they are applied sparingly — only to functions whose features tolerate overhead — because bogus-control-flow and flattening on a hot strcat loop would inflate runtime and binary size disproportionately for a program this tiny. All CorrectnessRisk weights are kept low-to-moderate since these passes are mature and the code is simple scalar/string logic with no fragile constructs (no inline asm, setjmp, or complex exception-dependent patterns expected beyond standard C++ overhead).
